For the Peacock cichlid Cichla monoculus, females attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of approximately 32 cm [Lp = approximately 32 cm], a milestone that marks the onset of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence. Field surveys conducted across the Amazon basin consistently report that spawning adults achieve an ultimate total length of 70 cm [Li = 70 cm], placing this species among the largest members of the Cichlinae. In tank-based growth trials, the wet weight at sexual maturity was estimated to be around 474 g [Wwp = around 474 g], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large sample of wild-caught individuals. The maximum adult wet weight recorded in the same dataset was 5118 g [Wwi = 5118 g], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required to reach full adult size. These mass-at-length relationships highlight the pronounced sexual size dimorphism characteristic of the genus, with gravid females often exceeding males in both length and mass during the breeding season.

Freshly hatched yolk-sac larvae of Cichla monoculus are particularly small, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.0042 g [Wwb = 0.0042 g], a value consistent with the small egg diameters typical of many neotropical cichlids. This extremely low birth mass imposes a narrow window for the yolk-sac larva to absorb its endogenous reserves and initiate exogenous feeding. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a water temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], the age at birth — defined operationally as the completion of yolk absorption, comprising an initial 2.5-day interval followed by 5.6 additional days of yolk-sac absorption — was observed to occur at 8.1 days [ab = 8.1 days]. The duration of this lecithotrophic phase is highly sensitive to thermal regime; higher temperatures accelerate metabolic demand and shorten the interval before first exogenous feeding. These observations align with general patterns in tropical cichlids, where rapid yolk utilization is an adaptation to warm, productive floodplain nurseries.

Reproductive output in Cichla monoculus has been quantified through both field observations and captive breeding studies. Females produce multiple clutches annually, with spawning events concentrated during the high-water season when prey availability peaks. Under optimal thermal conditions at a temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], the maximum reproduction rate was recorded as approximately 8.5 eggs per day when averaged across the year, a value that is notably high among South American cichlids and is thought to offset the heavy predation pressure experienced by both eggs and larvae in open-water habitats. The energetic demands of such sustained reproduction likely require females to maintain high feeding rates throughout the breeding period.

Longevity records for Cichla monoculus indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] under natural conditions, though this value is derived largely from otolith-based age estimates in populations from lenti at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]c environments. In cooler, less productive reservoirs, where metabolic costs are lower but growth is slower, individuals can survive for up to 8 years [am = up to 8 years] at a mean annual temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan is comparable to that of other large-bodied cichlid species, such as the congeneric Cichla temensis, and contrasts sharply with the shorter lives of smaller, more fecund cichlids. The extended duration of the adult phase allows for repeated spawning events across multiple seasons, reinforcing the iteroparous life-history strategy that characterizes this top predator. Senescence in this species is typically expressed as a gradual decline in reproductive output and swimming performance in the oldest age classes.

In comparative context, the life-history traits of Cichla monoculus align closely with predictions derived from its position as a large, piscivorous apex predator in neotropical river systems. The combination of a relatively modest size at puberty, 32 cm [Lp = 32 cm] total length, with a substantial ultimate length of 70 cm [Li = 70 cm], indicates that females allocate considerable post-maturation growth to somatic mass, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 5118 g [Wwi = 5118 g]. The contrast between the minute wet weight at birth of only 0.0042 g [Wwb = 0.0042 g] and the weight at puberty of 474 g [Wwp = 474 g] underscores a greater than five-order-of-magnitude increase in body mass from hatching to first reproduction. Such a rapid growth trajectory is energetically feasible only in the warm, prey-rich environments typical of Amazonian floodplains, where temperatures consistently near 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C] sustain elevated metabolic and feeding rates throughout the year.
